visual_features: A medium-sized langur with brownish-gray pelage, lighter on the ventral side than the dorsum. The tail is bicolored and the head has a distinct black crest on top, giving the 'mitered' appearance. Arms, legs, tail, and top of head range from light buttery yellow to bronze. The belly and inner thighs have white fur, creating a white collar effect around the neck. Black facial skin contrasted by pale pink eye rings. Weighs an average of 6.0 kg with males only slightly larger than females. Long forelimbs and relatively long hindlimbs adapted for leaping and brachiation. Neonates are white with a pale face and a dark reddish-brown spinal stripe.
description: The yellow-handed mitered langur (Presbytis melalophos), also known as the mitred leaf monkey or black-crested Sumatran langur, is a primate in the family Cercopithecidae native to Sumatra, Indonesia. There are four subspecies based on pelage differences, vocalizations, and geographic location. Like all members of the genus Presbytis, this species has evolved to digest cellulose through microbial fermentation in a specialized foregut. They are highly arboreal, spending most of their time in the forest understory, leaping between small branch supports. Groups consist of one male with five to seven females, with home ranges of 14–30 hectares.
population_estimate: No precise population estimate available. Population is declining due to extensive habitat loss, with 70% of their home range lost in the past decade according to some estimates. Listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
habitat: Lowland and submontane dipterocarp and evergreen rainforests of Sumatra, Indonesia. Found in southwestern Sumatra south of the Wampu and Simpang Kiri Rivers, and on Pini Island in the Batu Archipelago. Prefers discontinuous understory at approximately 90 ft (27 m) from the ground, but also found in the continuous main canopy and emergent layers. Can tolerate secondary forests and has been recorded in rubber plantations.
threats: Habitat loss due to oil palm plantation expansion — 70% of habitat lost in past decade
Habitat fragmentation leading to increased territorial conflict and home range overlap
ecosystem_role: As primarily frugivorous (50–60% of diet) and folivorous primates, they play a key role in seed dispersal and vegetation control. Feeds from up to 197 different tree species and prefers new leaves to mature leaves. Their selective feeding helps shape forest composition. They serve as prey for large predators including clouded leopards and pythons, and are part of a complex forest food web.
human_connection: Known locally as 'Simpai' in Malay. Their adaptability to secondary forests and rubber plantations offers some hope for coexistence with human development if sustainable practices are implemented. However, they are severely threatened by the palm oil industry, with the majority of their habitat lost to plantation expansion. They serve as an indicator species for forest health in Sumatra.
what_students_can_do: Advocate for wildlife-friendly and sustainable palm oil practices
Support conservation of Sumatran rainforests through reputable organizations
Study langur social behavior, communication, and dietary ecology
Raise awareness about the impact of deforestation on endemic Sumatran primates
fun_fact: Langur babies are born with whitish-gray fur and a single dark stripe down their back — this distinct coloration helps the troop spot and protect infants
They have multi-chambered 'ruminant-like' stomachs with specialized bacteria to break down cellulose from leaves
Groups typically consist of one male with five to seven females, living in home ranges of 14–30 hectares
Females determine the group's movement patterns and are responsible for initiating encounters with other groups, though they remain uninvolved in intergroup conflicts
There are four recognized subspecies based on pelage color variation, ranging from the whitest (P. m. bicolor) to the darkest (P. m. sumatrana)
